text_blocks.snippet: The first vaccine was developed by Edward Jenner in 1796, specifically against smallpox. He used material from cowpox sores to inoculate individuals, demonstrating that this provided protection against the more dangerous smallpox. This groundbreaking work laid the foundation for the field of vaccinology.
snippet_highlighted_words: developed by Edward Jenner in 1796, specifically against smallpox

list.title: Cowpox and Smallpox:
list.snippet: Jenner's insight was that individuals infected with cowpox, a relatively mild disease, were resistant to smallpox, a much more serious and often fatal illness.

list.title: Inoculation Experiment:
list.snippet: In 1796, Jenner famously inoculated an 8-year-old boy named James Phipps with material from a cowpox sore. Two months later, he exposed Phipps to smallpox, and the boy did not develop the disease.

list.title: Vaccination:
list.snippet: Jenner's method, later termed vaccination (from the Latin "vacca" for cow), involved using a mild disease (cowpox) to induce immunity against a more severe one (smallpox).

list.title: Impact:
list.snippet: Jenner's work was a monumental step in preventative medicine. Smallpox had been a devastating disease for centuries, and his vaccine eventually led to its global eradication.

list.title: Vaccinology:
list.snippet: Jenner's approach, using a related but less harmful pathogen to confer immunity, is the basis for many modern vaccines.
